utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, also good morning to the Defence. With me together with co-counsel Mrs. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Mr. Jose Doria, and -- as well as our acting case manager, Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I see that you wanted to show -- give a demonstration of inequality of arms. You are in full strength today. Yes, Madam Vidovic, appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we proceed? I see none. So as you know, today has -- today's sitting is going to be devoted to our oral decision pursuant to Rule 98 bis, as it has been amended on the 8th of December of last year. I will just state at the very beginning that the decision that I will be pronouncing on behalf of the Trial Chamber today is a unanimous decision on each and every point that I will be mentioning. The conclusions and the decisions have all been unanimous. You are aware that Rule 98 bis, as it now stands, as it now is, reads as follows: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count, if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." The Prosecution, as you are all aware, rested its case on the 31st of May and the Trial Chamber heard oral submissions or received oral submissions on the 2nd and on the 3rd of June respectively. Before proceeding any further, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to publicly recognise the high level of the submissions, oral submissions, made by both of you, the Prosecution and Defence, and equally the highly professional way in which you delivered them. Indeed the Trial Chamber also wishes to acknowledge in open -- in public session the efforts made by both parties since the inception of this case to make it possible for the Trial Chamber to conduct this trial in the smoothest manner possible and with the utmost celerity possible at the same time guaranteeing the full rights, both to the accused and to the Prosecution and, of course, without relegating the rights of victims and their plight to the background. I'll start first with the Rule 98 bis standard. This Chamber highlights that there is agreement between the parties that the last amendment to Rule 98 bis does not in any way change the standard of review to be applied by the Trial Chamber in its Rule 98 bis exercise which therefore remains that set out and repeatedly applied by these Trial Chambers, set out in the Jelisic appeals judgement. I will quote from the Jelisic appeals judgement because this would explain what the criterion is and the standard is: "The Appeals Chamber considers that the reference to Rule 98 bis to a situation in which the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction means a case in which in the opinion of the Trial Chamber the Prosecution evidence, if believed, is insufficient for any trier of fact to find that guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. In this respect, the Appeals Chamber follows its recent holding in the Delalic appeal judgement where it said the test applied is whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonable Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question. The capacity of the Prosecution evidence, if accepted, to sustain a conviction beyond reasonable doubt by a reasonable trier of fact is the key concept. Thus the test is not whether the trier would in fact arrive at the conviction beyond reasonable doubt, on the Prosecution evidence, if accepted, but whether it could, at the close of the case for the Prosecution, the Chamber may find that the Prosecution evidence is sufficient to sustain a conviction beyond reasonable doubt, and yet, even if no Defence evidence is subsequently adduced, proceed to acquit at the end of the trial if in its own view of the evidence, the Prosecution has not in fact proved the guilt beyond reasonable doubt." Now, the Trial Chamber has examined all the evidence tendered by the Prosecution, as well as the documents that have been exhibited by the Defence, and has applied this standard when considering each one of the six counts contained in the Oric indictment, and comes to the following conclusions. I will start first with the legal requirements for Article 3 under the ICTY Statute, and that will give you an idea of the law that we applied before reaching our conclusions. The Accused is charged under second -- the second amended indictment with six counts of violations of the laws and customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and the Accused is precisely charged with murder and cruel treatment pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute and Common Article 3(1)(A) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. He is then also charged with wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, not justified by military necessity and with plunder of public or private property pursuant to Article 3(B) and (E) of the Statute respectively. Accordingly, the very first exercise that we carried out was to establish what are the legal requirements for Article 3 of the Statute to subsist and then proceed to establish case by case whether for the purposes of Rule 98 the Prosecution has reached the standard to which I referred to earlier. Article 3 of the Statute is entitled "Violations of the laws or customs of war." The expression or this expression is a traditional term of art used in the past which has now largely been replaced by the more recent and comprehensive notion of international humanitarian law. Article 3 of the Statute thus constitutes a residual clause covering all violations of humanitarian law not falling under Articles 2, 4 or 5 of the Statute, including but not limited to violations of the Hague law on international conflicts and violations of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 to which later on I will be referring to as Common Article 3. For an offence to be adjudicated under Article 3 of the Statute, a state of armed conflict must have existed at the time of the -- at the time the offence was committed and, in addition, the offence must be closely related to the -- the offence must be closely related to the armed conflict. I shall deal next with the existence of an armed conflict, and this is the legal part first, and then I will come to facts and findings later. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal an armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state. The legal position as we see it with regard to the nexus that is required between the acts of the accused and the armed conflict, this is what we have to say. The requirement that the acts of the accused be closely related to the armed conflict does not necessitate that the offence be committed whilst fighting is actually taking place or at the scene of combat. The laws of war apply and continue to apply to the whole of the territory under the control of one of the parties to the conflict whether or not actual combat takes place there until a general conclusion of peace or a peaceful settlement is achieved. The armed conflict need not have been the cause of the commission of the crime but the existence of an armed conflict must, at a minimum, have played a substantial part in the perpetrator's ability to commit it. His decision to commit it, the manner in which it was committed, or the purpose for which it was committed. That requirement would be fulfilled inter alia if the offence was committed either during or in the aftermath of the fighting provided that it is committed in furtherance of or at least under the guise of the situation created by the fighting. There are then in this context the so-called four Tadic conditions which must be satisfied before we can -- before this Trial Chamber or any other Chamber can ultimately convict an accused under Article 3 of the Statute. In the Tadic Jurisdiction Decision, the Appeals Chamber indicated that for a rule of international humanitarian law to fall under Article 3 of the Statute, the following conditions or requirements need to exist or be satisfied. First, the violation must constitute an infringement of a rule of international law. Second, the rule must be customary in nature or if it belongs to treaty law, the required conditions must be met. Third, the violation must be serious, and last but not least, the fourth, the violation of the rule must entail under customary or conventional law the individual criminal responsibility of the person breaching the rule. What comes next is in relation to counts 1 and 2 only, but an additional requirement for the applicability of Article 3 of the Statute, as it relates to counts 1 and 2 of the indictment, is, according to jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that the underlying violation must have been committed against persons taking no active part in the hostilities. In view of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, this requirement extends to any individual not taking part in hostilities, including members of the armed forces who have laid down their arms, and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention or any other cause. Because of the various submissions that we have heard from both of you, I need to address also a few further legal considerations. The charges of murder and cruel treatment in counts 1 and 2 are brought under Common Article 3. It is undisputed that Article 3 of the Statute covers violations of Common Article 3. Common Article 3 which has acquired the status of customary international law applies regardless of the international or internal character of the armed conflict, because as affirmed by this Tribunal in the Celebici case, and this is the Appeals Chamber speaking, the principles enshrined therein are so fundamental that they are regarded as governing both internal and international conflict. The charges of wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, not justified by military necessity and plunder of public or private property are specifically enumerated in paragraphs B and C respectively of Article 3 of the Statute as violations of the laws or customs of war. They are in turn based on the 1907 Hague Convention, convention 4, respecting the laws and customs of war on land and the regulations annexed to it which have become rules of international customary law, as you know, and these have been interpreted and applied by the Nuremberg Tribunal. The Defence argues that because the charges of wanton destruction and plunder derive from The Hague rule or Hague law they only apply in an international armed conflict and that there is no warrant - I'm quoting from the Defence pre-trial brief - there is no warrant for considering that Articles 3(B) and (E) apply in an internal conflict. The Trial Chamber makes it clear at the outset that the issue of the -- of application of the prohibition of wanton destruction and plunder pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute to internal armed conflicts has been resolved already in the affirmative by the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. The Appeals Chamber held that customary international law as it had developed at the relevant time did not allow for the extent of protection of civilian property against destruction to vary depending on the nature of the conflict. The same is true for the prohibition of plunder which is prohibited under customary international law irrespective of whether the conflict in question is internal or international. I now come to the facts and findings of this Trial Chamber in relation to the various points that I have dealt with. I will deal first with facts and findings relating to the existence of an armed conflict. The Prosecution alleges that at all times relevant to the indictment, that is between the 10th of June 1992 to the 20th of March 1993 a state of armed conflict existed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, is capable of proving beyond reasonable doubt that a state of armed conflict indeed existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the said period of time. The testimony of Pyers Tucker, of and Andrew James Gow, of Becir Bogilovic, of General Sead Delic, and a large number of exhibited documents are at the basis of the Trial Chamber's conclusion. As regards the nexus between the acts of the accused and the armed conflict, as regards this, we have to say the following: The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, is capable of proving beyond reasonable doubt such nexus. In reaching this conclusion, the Trial Chamber has considered the testimony of Pyers Tucker, of Andrew James Gow, of Becir Bogilovic, of Nedret Mujkanovic of Slavoljub Zikic, of Slavisa Eric, of Branislav Gligic, of General Sead Delic, and a large number of exhibited documents in which the accused's name features in relation to the armed conflict and some of the events thereof. As regards the four Tadic conditions, I've already stated that Common Article 3 of the -- to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the rules contained in the 1907 Hague Conventions form part of customary international law. In view of this the Trial Chamber finds that there can be no doubt and that the first and second Tadic conditions are satisfied. With regard to the third and fourth Tadic conditions, the Trial Chamber has no doubt that the crimes of murder and cruel treatment breach a rule protecting important values and involve grave consequences for the victims. As regards the crime of wanton destruction under Article 3(B) of the Statute, the Trial Chamber considers that the destruction must be both serious in relation to an individual object, as well as cover a substantial range of a particular city, town, or village. Since one of the requirements of this crime is that the damage be on a large scale, it follows that this also satisfies the third Tadic condition. As regards the seriousness of plunder, under Article 3 of the Statute, the Trial Chamber observes that the acquisition or appropriation of property must cause grave consequences for the victims. We have no doubt at all that the offence of plunder, under Article 3(E) of the Statute, constitutes a serious violation of international humanitarian law and therefore satisfies the third Tadic condition. As regards the fourth Tadic condition, in relation to all the crimes with which the Accused stands charged, the case law of this Tribunal has repeatedly affirmed that these entail individual criminal responsibility under international law. This, the fourth Tadic condition, is therefore also satisfied. Relating to the additional requirement under Common Article 3 which is important for the purposes of counts 1 and 2, it is the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, could prove beyond reasonable doubt that those who were allegedly killed or were subjected to cruel treatment as alleged in the indictment were persons taking no active part in the hostilities at the relevant time. The basis for the Trial Chamber's conclusion with regard to both murder and cruel treatment rests mainly on the testimony of the witnesses who, according to the indictment, were the victims of cruel treatment. I will now come to count 1, which is one of murder, being a violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute and recognised by Article 3(1)(A) of the Geneva Conventions. The definition of murder as a violations of the laws or customs of war is now settled in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber adopts the following elements of the crime of murder. First, that the person is dead. Second, that the death was caused by an act or omission of the accused or of a person or persons for whose acts or omissions the accused bears criminal responsibility. As regards the actus reus of murder, this consists in the action or omission of the perpetrator resulting in the death of the person. Ultimately the Prosecution needs to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the perpetrators conduct contributed substantially to the death of the person. Proof beyond reasonable doubt that the person was murdered does not necessarily require that the dead body of that person has been retrieved or recovered. The fact of a person's death can be inferred circumstantially from all of the evidence presented to the Trial Chamber provided that the only reasonable inference is that the person is dead as a result of the acts or omissions of the perpetrator. Intent is required to fulfil the mens rea of murder. The mens rea for murder is satisfied when the act was done or the omission was made by the perpetrator or a person or persons for whose acts or omissions the accused bears responsibility with an intent to kill or to inflict grievous bodily harm or serious injury in the reasonable knowledge and with the acceptance that such act or omission was more likely than not to cause death. In the Celebici case, the Trial Chamber held that there was no difference in the mens rea requirement for wilful killing being a grave breach of the 1949 Geneva Conventions pursuant to Article 2 of the Statute and murder being a violation of the laws or customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. The mens rea is the same. The Trial Chamber also holds that intent includes what has on occasions been referred to in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal as dolus eventualis, defined as comprising both knowledge of the risk and acceptance of the risk. Negligence and gross negligence do not satisfy the requirement for intent. However, since the following point was raised by the Defence, the Trial Chamber adopts the approach of other Trial Chambers in holding that premeditation is not a requirement for establishing the mental element or the formal element of the crime of murder. I now come to the facts and findings relating to murder. For the purpose of count 1, the Prosecution alleges that the following persons were killed or murdered: Dragutin Kukic, Jakov Dokic, Dragan Ilic, Milisav Milovanovic, Kostadin Popovic, Branko Sekulic, and Bogdan Zivanovic. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that there is evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that both the actus reus and the mens rea for murder have been demonstrated in all cases except for that relating to the alleged death of Bogdan Zivanovic, for whom no evidence capable of supporting a conviction has been adduced. This exception has also been acknowledged by the Prosecution in the course of their submissions of the 3rd of June 2005. In reaching this conclusion, the Trial Chamber mainly relies on the testimony of Nedjeljko Radic, Andja Radovic, Vidosav Dzokic, Witness C007, Vojka Milovanovic, and Nikola Popovic. I now come to 7(3) -- Article 7(3) responsibility, that is command responsibility. In fact what remains to be seen in relation to count 1 is whether, as regards Article 7(3) responsibility, which is the only kind of criminal responsibility charged against the Accused in count 1, the Prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence capable of sustaining a conviction. The Prosecution alleges that the Accused from about September 1992 to August 1995 knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to plan, prepare or execute the imprisonment, killing and/or cruel treatment of Serbs detained at the Srebrenica police station and the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building or had done so and he failed to take the necessary it and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. The principle of superior criminal responsibility for failure to prevent or punish crimes committed by subordinates is well established, as you all know, in conventional and customary law applicable to both international and internal armed conflicts. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal requires three elements to be established, to be satisfied, for the existence of superior criminal responsibility. First, that there is a superior-subordinate relationship between the accused and the perpetrators. Second, that the accused knew or had reason to know that a crime had been or was about to be committed by the perpetrators. And third, that the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of the crime or punish the perpetrators thereof. I will deal with these three elements sequitur, one by one, one after the other. The Trial Chamber recalls that the doctrine of command responsibility is ultimately predicated on the power of the superior to control the acts of his subordinates. Individuals in position of authority may incur criminal responsibility under the doctrine of command responsibility on the basis of their de jure as well as de facto positions as superiors. The superior may be a military commander but he may also be a civilian authority. According to the case law of this Tribunal, whereas a formal appointment is an important aspect to consider for command responsibility, de facto control in the absence of de facto -- de jure authority may suffice for the purpose of incurring criminal responsibility. It is noteworthy that in many conflicts there may be only de facto self-proclaimed governments with their de facto armies and paramilitary groups. Thus the perpetrator that -- thus -- that the perpetrator was the subordinate of the accused of -- of an accused does not import a requirement of direct or formal subordination. Likewise the mere temporary nature of a military unit does not per se exclude a relationship of subordination between the members of the unit and its Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander. What is decisive in determining criminal liability under Article 7(3) is whether the superior wields effective control over the persons committing the underlying violations of international humanitarian law, in the sense of having the material ability to prevent or punish the commission of these offences. In this regard, substantial influence by itself is not indicative of a sufficient degree of control. It would have to meet the threshold of effective control. Whether the superior has the requisite level of control is a matter which must be determined on the basis of the evidence presented at trial. The Defence differs from this position in so far as it submits that identification of persons who committed crimes must be established. However, in the Trial Chamber's view, in order to ascertain the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship, identification of the perpetrators, for instance through their names, is not required in order to prove the superior's effective control over the -- those perpetrators. However, it must be established at least that the individual who committed the crime was within a unit or a group under the control of the superior. The second element, knew or had reason to know. A superior must -- may possess the mens rea required to incur criminal liability under Article 7(3) of the Statute where, first, he had actual knowledge established through direct or circumstantial evidence that his subordinates were committing or about to commit a crime under Article 3 of the Statute in this case, or, secondly, that he had information which would put him on notice of such offences by his subordinates. In the absence of direct evidence, the superior's actual knowledge that his subordinates were committing or about to commit crimes cannot be presumed. It must be established by way of circumstantial evidence. According to the case law of this Tribunal, there are several indicia which the Trial Chamber may consider in reaching its conclusion, and these have been considered by us. What constitutes the standard had reason to know has been discussed at length in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. In this regard the Defence claims that the Accused had no specific information in his possession providing notice of the risk of offences having been committed or about to be committed, the Trial Chamber notes that the Celebici trial judgement states that a superior can be held responsible, criminally responsible, if some specific information was in fact available to him which would have put him on notice of offences committed by his subordinates. However, it explained that this information need not be such that can by itself lead to the conclusion of the existence of such crimes. This finding has been refined by the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, to which -- to mean that a superior must have had some general information in his possession which would put him on notice of unlawful acts by his subordinates. Such information may be written or oral but does not need to have the form of specific reports submitted, nor to provide specific information about unlawful acts committed or about to be committed. The Trial Chamber concurs with this interpretation. As regards the third element, necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish. A legal duty exists upon superiors to take all the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of crimes or if crimes have been committed to punish the perpetrators but a superior may only be held responsible for failing to take measures that are within his powers, in other words those that are within his material possibility. The duty to prevent or punish does not provide the Accused with alternative and equally satisfying options but with two distinct sets of obligations. The duty to prevent rests on a superior at any time before the commission of a crime by a subordinate if he acquires knowledge that such a crime is being prepared or planned, or when he has reasonable grounds to suspect that such crimes are being or may be committed. The duty to punish arises only after a crime has been committed. An Accused cannot be found liable under the principle of superior responsibility for crimes committed by a subordinate before the said Accused assumed command over that subordinate. The Trial Chamber affirms that in conformity with the principle that nemo ad impossibilia tenetur, a superior is not obliged to perform the impossible. It is the accused's degree of effective control, if at all, over his subordinates which has guided and will continue to guide the Trial Chamber in determining whether he took the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crime or to punish a perpetrator of the crime. As held in the Blaskic Appeals Judgement, there is no hard and fast rule as to what at law constitutes necessary and reasonable measures because this ultimately depends on the particular evidence in each case. This is important for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis exercise. Lastly, before I come to the facts, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal has consistently held that the existence of a causal nexus between a superior's failure to prevent a subordinate's crime and the occurrence of these crimes is not necessary in order to establish the third element of Article 7(3). The Trial Chamber concurs with this view. This is the law in relation to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Now I come to the facts and findings for the purpose of Rule 98 bis. The -- I will deal first with facts and findings relating to superior-subordinate relationship. In the majority of the alleged murders in count 1 of the indictment, it is not possible to identify each individual perpetrator from the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. Dragutin Kukic is alleged to have been killed in the Srebrenica police station while the rest were supposedly killed in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. The approach taken by the Trial Chamber therefore has been to establish if, for the purpose of and within the parameters of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, could lead the trier of fact to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused had de jure or where this is not shown, de facto superior authority over the guards at the Srebrenica police station and in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. The Trial Chamber has considered all the relevant evidence and comes to the conclusion that there is sufficient evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that there existed at least a de facto superior-subordinate relationship between the accused and the alleged perpetrators at the Srebrenica police station in September 1992 when Dragutin Kukic was allegedly killed. Similarly, the Trial Chamber also comes to the conclusion that there is sufficient evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that there existed at least a de facto superior-subordinate relationship between the accused and the alleged perpetrators at the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building between 6th February and 20th March of 1993 when the other persons I already mentioned were allegedly killed. There is also evidence which suggests a de jure superior-subordinate relationship but this will be one of the hard nuts to crack when the trial comes to final judgement and the Trial Chamber will not go into it now as what has been established suffices for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusions on the evidence of Slavoljub Zikic, Svetlana Trifunovic, Ratko Nikolic, Ilija Ivanovic, Becir Bogilovic, Nedret Mujkanovic, Hakija Meholjic, Mensud Omerovic, Pyers Tucker, and General Sead Delic. The Trial Chamber also makes reference to Exhibit P329 in part 3 of it, where the accused is reported as saying that that the commander of the military police and the detention centre was Mirzet Halilovic as well as Exhibit P458. Findings as regards actual or imputed knowledge of the accused of the killings. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose and within the parameters of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution lass adduced evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had actual or imputed knowledge of the killing of Dragutin Kukic allegedly committed at the Srebrenica police station in September 1992. The Trial Chamber bases itself mainly on the evidence of Nedjeljko Radic. Similarly the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of and within the parameters of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of facts could hold beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused had actual knowledge or imputed knowledge of the killing of the other persons I mentioned earlier, allegedly committed at the building beyond the Srebrenica municipal building between the 6th February and the 20th March of 1993. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusions mainly on the testimony of Milenija Mitrovic, Stana Stamenic, Ilija Ivanovic and Pyers Tucker. As regards the failure by the Accused to prevent or punish the said killings, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that the Prosecution has adduced evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact would hold beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused failed to prevent or punish the crimes of murder as charged in count 1. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusions that there is such evidence regarding the alleged failure to prevent on the evidence of Nedjeljko Radic but mainly on Exhibit P329. As regards the alleged allegation that the accused failed to punish, the Trial Chamber rests -- mainly considered Exhibit P329 in its third part. Conclusion of the Trial Chamber on count 1. The Trial Chamber therefore comes to the conclusion that there is sufficient evidence upon which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused under Article 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal of the murders mentioned in paragraph 25 in the indictment to which count 1 refers with the exception of the alleged murder of Bogdan Zivanovic. I now come to count 2, cruel treatment, this being a violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Article 3 and 7(3) of the Statute and recognised by Article 3(1)(A) of the Geneva Conventions. The Trial Chamber adopts the following elements for the crime of cruel treatment. First, an act or omission causing serious mental suffering or serious physical suffering or serious injury or constituting a serious attack on human dignity. Second, such act or omission is committed with the intent to cause serious mental suffering or serious physical suffering or serious injury or a serious attack on human dignity. The Trial Chambers of this Tribunal have consistently recognised that the actus reus of cruel treatment in an internal armed conflict under Article 3 is equivalent to inhumane treatment in an international armed conflict under Article 2. The serious mental suffering or serious physical suffering or serious injury or serious attack on human dignity should be assessed taking into account both objective factors concerning the severity of the said conduct and the subjective factors relating to the particular victim. The Trial Chamber points out that the mens rea for cruel treatment under Article 3 of the Statute is the same as the mens rea for inhumane acts under Article 5 of the Statute. The required mens rea is met where the accused at the time of the act or of the omission had the intention to inflict serious mental suffering or serious physical sufferings or serious injury or a serious attack on -- upon human dignity of the person or where he knew and accepted that his act or omission was more likely than not to cause one of the mentioned sufferings or injuries. As in the case of the intent required for the crime of murder, the Trial Chamber holds that the intent includes dolus eventualis, defined as comprising both knowledge of the risk and acceptance of it. I come to fact and findings. For the purpose of count 2, the Prosecution alleges that the following persons were cruelly treated. First, between 24 September 1992 and 16 October 1992, at the Srebrenica police station, first Nedjeljko Radic and Slavoljub Zikic, Zoran Brankovic, Nevenko Bubanj, Veselin Sarac, and then between the 15th of December 1992 and the 20th March, initially in the police station and thereafter at the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building, Ilija Ivanovic, Ratko Nikolic, Rado Pejic, Stanko Mitrovic, Miloje Obradovic and Mile Trifunovic. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that there is evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that both the actus reus and the mens rea for cruel treatment have been demonstrated beyond reasonable doubt in all cases except that relating to Miloje Obradovic, for whom no evidence capable of supporting a conviction has been adduced. Of course, this is being said only for the purpose of Rule 98 bis; that is, on a prima facie basis. This exception that I have mentioned relating to Mile Obradovic has been acknowledged by the Prosecution in the course of their submission of the 3rd June 2005. In reaching this conclusion, the Trial Chamber mainly relies on the testimony of Nedjeljko Radic, Slavoljub Zigic, Ilija Ivanovic, Andja Radovic, Branimir Mitrovic, Svetlana Trifunovic, Pyers Tucker, Witness C007, and Exhibits P43, 83, 384, 386, 454, 464, and 476. I will now deal with Article 7(3), responsibility. As in the case of count 1, what remains to be seen is whether, as regards Article 7(3), command responsibility, which is hereto the only kind of criminal responsibility charged against the accused in count 2, the Prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence capable of sustaining a conviction if believed within the parameters of the Rule 98 bis standard that I referred to earlier. The Prosecution alleges that the accused from about September 1992 to August 1995 knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to plan, prepare or execute the imprisonment, killing or cruel treatment of Serbs detained at the Srebrenica police station and the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building or had done so and he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent acts -- such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. I have already explained the Trial Chamber's position on the principle of superior criminal responsibility for failure to prevent or punish crimes committed by subordinates when dealing with count 1 and what I said then applies also to count 2 and therefore need not be repeated. Therefore, I shall pass on immediately to the Trial Chamber's findings. Findings as regard superior subordinate relationship. As in the case of count 1, even in count 2, it is not possible to identify each individual perpetrator from the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. Even here, therefore, the approach taken by the Trial Chamber has been to establish if, for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, could lead the trier of fact, a reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had de jure or where this is not shown, de facto superior authority over the guards at the Srebrenica police station and in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. The Trial Chamber has considered all the evidence which is relevant and comes to the same conclusion it reached in this context for the purpose of count 1, namely that there is sufficient evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that there existed at least a de facto superior-subordinate relationship between the Accused and the alleged perpetrators at the Srebrenica police station in September and October 1992, and at the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building between the 15th of December 1992 and the 20th of March 1993. There is also evidence which suggests a de jure subordinate relation, but as I said earlier this will be left to be considered when this trial comes to final judgement. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusion on the same evidence as that pointed out in the case of count 1. Findings as regards actual or imputed knowledge of the accused or cruel -- of the cruel treatment. As in the case of count 1, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of and within the parameters of Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution has adduced evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had actual or imputed knowledge of the cruel treatment inflicted on the persons mentioned in paragraphs -- paragraph 24 of the indictment, in the relevant two buildings and -- to which count 2 refers. The Trial Chamber bases itself mainly on the evidence of Nedjeljko Radic, that is of Milenija Mitrovic, Stana Stanisic, Ilija Ivanovic, and Pyers Tucker. Findings as regards -- as regards the failure by the accused to prevent or punish the said cruel treatment, the Trial Chamber comes to the same conclusion it reached for the purposes of count 1, namely that the Prosecution has adduced evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that the accused failed to prevent or punish the crimes of cruel treatment as charged in count 2. Again, even in the case of count 2, the Trial Chamber bases its conclusion that there is such evidence regarding the alleged failure to prevent on the evidence of Nedjeljko Radic but mainly on Exhibit P329, and as regards his alleged failure to punish on Exhibit P329. This is therefore our conclusion on count 2. Trial Chamber therefore comes to the conclusion that there is sufficient evidence upon which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused under Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal, of the cruel treatment mentioned in paragraph 24 of the indictment to which count 2 refers, with the exception of the alleged cruel treatment of Miloje Obradovic. We will deal now with counts 3 and 5, wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, not justified by military necessity, and we will deal with them together, and then we will dispose of the question relating to the different kinds of imputed criminal responsibility separately. The Prosecution has charged the accused with the offence of wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, not justified by military necessity. In count 3, it is alleged that the accused is criminally responsible as a commander pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for all incidents of destruction contained in the indictment. In count 5, the Prosecution also charged the Accused with individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute, for the destructions or -- but only for the destructions that occurred during the attacks on Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica, and Jezestica, in which the accused according to the indictment is alleged to have participated in person. Wanton destruction of cities, towns offer villages or devastation not justified by military necessary si is listed as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3(B) of the Statute. Article 3(B) of the Statute is in turn based on the 1907 Hague regulations which prohibit the destruction trucks and seizure of enemy property unless imperatively demanded by the necessities of war. The provision was restated in Article 6(B) of the Nuremberg charter and in principle 6 of the Nuremberg principles. The Trial Chamber has no doubt at all that the crime described in Article 3(B) of our Statute formed part of customary international law at the time it was -- the relative crime was allegedly committed. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the crime of wanton destruction consists of the following elements: First the destruction of the property occurred on a large scale; second, the destruction was not justified by military necessity; and third, the perpetrator acted with the intent, including dolus eventualis to destroy the property in question. The protection afforded by Article 3(B) of our Statute includes all property in the territory involved in the conflict, including that located in enemy territory and in territory not under effective occupation. I have already stated earlier on that the Trial Chamber holds that the provisions of Article 3(B) of the Statute apply both to international as well as to internal conflicts. I shall briefly deal with these three elements one by one. Extent of the destruction. The Trial Chamber considers that in order to constitute a violation of the laws or customs of war, the destruction must both serious in relation to an individual object, and cover substantial range of a particular city, town, or village. The sporadic or isolated destruction of houses of a settlement is insufficient to fulfil the qualifications of the crime in question. Regarding the extent of the destruction, the Prosecution contends that the crime of wanton destruction is perpetrated with even the partial destruction of cities, towns or villages. It maintains that there is no requirement in international humanitarian law that any of these settlements must be destroyed in its entirety. The Defence opposes this interpretation in its pre-trial brief, emphasising that the provision makes no reference to partial destruction. The Defence also submitted that there is no precise record of the buildings destroyed and that in the state of the evidence available, there is no way that the Trial Chamber can come to the conclusion that the Prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence to assess the extent of the damage. The Trial Chamber agrees with the Prosecution's submissions insofar as it would amount to an overly narrow reading of the prohibition of wanton destruction to require proof of the total destruction of a city, town or village. The Trial Chamber in reaching its decision has therefore considered on a case-by-case basis, whether the extent of the destruction of each particular relevant village or hamlet that has been proven can be regarded as substantial enough in relation to the overall category under consideration. In doing so, it has also kept in mind the other submission of the Defence that the evidence is insufficient. Our position on military necessity. The Trial Chamber notes that the absence of military necessity is explicitly mentioned in the actus reus of wanton destruction pursuant to Article 3(B) of the Statute; hence, it must be considered a negative element of the crime. As like for other elements of the crime, it is for the Prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that this requirement has been met. The Prosecution submits that the destruction of property was not justified by military necessity and that none of the destroyed objects was a legitimate target. Rather, the destruction is said to have occurred as a result of deliberate attacks directed at civilian objects. The Defence disagrees and states Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the attacks referred to in the indictment constituted legitimate actions against military or otherwise strategic targets with some of the destruction that may have been caused constituting collateral damage. A definition of what can constitute a military objective is given by Article 52 of the 1977 additional protocol 1 to the Geneva Conventions. Namely, those objects which by their nature, location, purpose or use make an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralisation in the circumstances ruling at the time offers a definite military advantage. The Trial Chamber agrees with the Galic Trial Chamber that an object shall not and should not be attacked when it is not reasonable to believe in the circumstances of the person contemplating the attack, including the information available to him, that the object is being used to make an effective contribution to military action. Our position on the mens rea. The Trial Chamber finds that the mental state required for an accused to be convicted of the crime under Article 3(B) of the Statute is the intent to destroy mentioned, including dolus eventualis, which, as I stated earlier, is defined as foreseeability of the consequences of there conduct -- of the conduct and the acceptance of the results as its very likely consequence. I now come to the findings. The indictment in paragraphs 30 to 34 alleges that Bosnian Serb buildings, dwellings, and other property in the following Bosnian Serb villages were wantonly destroyed. On the 21st and 27th June 1992, the village of Ratkovici, including the surrounding hamlets of Bradjevina, Ducice, and Gornji Ratkovici. On 8 August 1992, the village of Jezestica, and the hamlet of Bozici. On 5th October 1992, the village of Fakovici, including the surrounding hamlets of Radijevici and Divovici. Between 14th and 19th December 1992, the village or town of Bjelovac and the adjoining hamlet of Sikirici. And lastly, on the 7th and 8th January 1993, the village of Kravica and the two nearby villages of Siljkovici and Jezestica. Having examined all the relevant evidence tendered by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion that there is evidence on the basis of which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could hold beyond reasonable doubt that the crime of wanton destruction, not justified by military necessity occurred in all the villages and hamlets named -- just named, except for the villages of Radijevici and Bozici, both in the Bratunac municipality. In these two villages, the evidence adduced by the Prosecution does not appear to be sufficient to meet the large-scale requirement of the destruction. Incidentally, the Prosecution concedes that insufficient evidence has been adduced with regard to these two villages. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusion mainly on the testimony of Miljenko Stevanovic, Branislav Gligic, Vaselko Bogidjevic [phoen], Stanislav Stevanovic, Dragan Juric, Miladin Simic, Milo Rankovic, Dragomir Miladinovic, Milodin Bogdanovic [phoen], Slavka Djokic, Novka Bozic [phoen], Slavoljub Zikic, Slavka Martic, Slavoljub Filipovic, Slavisa Eric, and Rato Nikolic. What remains to be seen is the presence of criminal responsibility as alleged by the Prosecution but of course, this exercise we have done only for the purpose of Rule 98 bis. I shall start first with Article 7(3), command responsibility as brought against the Accused in count 3 of the indictment. The Prosecution alleges that the Accused, from about June 1992 to August 1995, knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit such wanton destruction or had done so in the specified villages and hamlets on or about the indicated dates and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. Earlier on, when dealing with count 1, I explained extensively the Trial Chamber's position on the concept of superior criminal responsibility for failure to prevent or punish crimes committed by subordinates and what I said then applies to count 3 and therefore I am not going to repeat it. I am therefore going to pass on immediately to the Trial Chamber's findings. Findings with regard to superior-subordinate relationship. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that there is evidence which, if believed, is sufficient to prove beyond reasonable doubt or -- that the Muslim forces in Srebrenica which allegedly participated in the attacks during which the wanton destruction is alleged to have occurred, operated in some sort of organised structure and that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had structures, command and control arrangements and the degree and ordering of communication -- and ordering, as early as April 1992. This conclusion is of course being reached on a prima facie basis and only within the standard requirements of Article -- of Rule 98 bis. There is also evidence which, if believed, could tend to prove beyond reasonable doubt that by the end of 1992 and early 1993, operations led by the Accused could be considered within the framework of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is also evidence which, if believed, could tend to show beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused was first appointed commander of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence staff and later commander of the joint armed forces of the subregion. There is also evidence which, if believed, would tend to show beyond reasonable doubt that, although sometimes disputed, the Accused's authority over local commanders in the Srebrenica area did indeed exist and that local commanders saw him as their commander. In other words, that he had real and effective control. There is also evidence which if believed would show beyond reasonable doubt some kind of organised military structure in which the attacks on the villages and hamlets mentioned in the indictment were planned and executed. There is also evidence that although in the great majority of cases the perpetrators are not identified by name, they are sufficiently recognised as being fighters or soldiers and this is adduced in a way in which, if believed, could sustain beyond reasonable doubt the argument that the Accused had a superior-subordinate relationship with members of these units. In reaching these conclusions, the Trial Chamber relies mainly on the testimony of James Gow on the General Sead Delic, of Nedret Mujkanovic, of Pyers Tucker, Hakija Meholjic, of Branislav Gligic, and on Exhibits P82, 267, and 84, some of the intercepts, particularly P358, 352, 355, 359, 363, 361, 362, 270, and last but not least, on the accused's own interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, P328 and 329. In sum, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis and for this purpose only, the Prosecution has reached the standard required in relation to this first element of Article 7(3) responsibility. Our findings with regard to the actual or imputed knowledge of the accused of the wanton destruction. Here, too, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion that the accused had actual or imputed knowledge of the alleged wanton destruction. The Trial Chamber relies mainly on the evidence of Hakija Meholjic, Milenko Stevanovic, Stanisa Stevanovic, Dragomir Miladinovic, Mira Stojanovic, Pyers Tucker, and of Nedret Mujkanovic, as well as on Exhibits P84, P87, P89, P2 and P267. As regards the alleged failure by the accused to prevent or punish the said wanton destruction, our findings are as follows: Upon examining the totality of the relevant evidence, we come -- we have come to the conclusion that the Prosecution has adduced evidence which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion that the Accused failed to prevent or punish the perpetrators for the alleged wanton destruction. The Trial Chamber relies mainly on the evidence of Nedret Mujkanovic as well as on exhibits P270, 362, 351 and 84, unless I say "D," it means that these are all Prosecution exhibits so that I don't have to repeat each time "P." You now tomorrow cot charged individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. This type of criminal responsibility is charged against the accused in count 5 which limits it to wanton destruction allegedly caused during the attacks on Fakovici, on 5th October 1992, that on Bjelovac between the 14th and the 19th of December 1992, and finally that on Kravica and Jezestica which allegedly took place on the 7th and 8th of January 1993. We have already decided that there is sufficient evidence which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion beyond reasonable doubt that wanton destruction in terms and for the purpose of Article 3 of the Statute occurred in these places on or about the said dates for the sole purpose of Rule 98 bis. In paragraph 37 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that the Accused implemented a strategy of wanton destruction to achieve his objectives and that accordingly, he did not make any or sufficient orders to prevent such wanton destruction. The Prosecution alleges that he failed to address the issue of wanton destruction and plunder at the briefing of operations, and that he personally took part in each of these attacks. According to the Prosecution, the Accused continuously failed to make any or sufficient orders to prevent wanton destruction of property and that these acts and omissions instigated the commission of the crimes and aided and abetted the perpetrators to commit such unlawful and wanton destruction, not justified by military necessity. To the great surprise of the Trial Chamber, not to mention the even greater one which was more than apparent on the bewildered faces of Defence counsel, during the oral submissions made by lead counsel for the Prosecution during the sitting of 3rd June, we learnt for the first time that the Prosecution was maintaining that the Article 7(1) individual criminal responsibility charged under count 5 included not only instigation and aiding and abetting, but planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of the wanton destruction. The same submission has been made in relation to count 6 which deals with the crime of plunder. When asked to substantiate this submission, lead counsel for the Prosecution referred to paragraph 12 of the indictment where it is stated as follows: Individual criminal responsibility includes planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of any acts or omissions set forth in the indictment. What learned lead counsel for the Prosecution obviously failed to consider fully is what follows immediately after this particular segment in the same paragraph 12, namely, and I'm quoting, "Naser Oric's continued failure to take reasonable measures to prevent wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, and to punish the perpetrators it would committed such crimes as well as his active involvement in the attacks during which such wanton destruction was caused, instigated the commission of the crimes and aided and abetted the perpetrators of these crimes." In the firm belief of this Trial Chamber, even from the reading of paragraph 12 on the indictment alone, it should have sufficed to understand that while in the first of those two sentences, the concept of individual criminal responsibility is being described and affirmed in general terms, the second sentence specifies which specific areas of individual criminal responsibility the accused is being charged with. We hardly need to emphasise that this is how it should be, especially in the light of the constant and uniform jurisprudence of this Tribunal that an indictment needs to be specific when it comes to the kind of acts and omissions underlying the criminal -- underlying the criminal responsibility the Accused is charged with. That this is precisely the position emerges then in the most obvious manner when we come to counts 5 and 6 themselves, and paragraph 37, upon which they are predicated. In paragraph 37 of the indictment, we read, Naser Oric continuously failed to make any or sufficient orders to prevent wanton destruction and plunder of property. These acts and omissions instigated the commission of the crimes and aided and abetted the perpetrators to commit such unlawful and wanton destruction, not justified by military necessity and plunder. These words according to us leave no doubt that in the sphere of 7(1) -- Article 7(1) responsibility, the accused is only being charged with having instigated and aided and abetted the said crimes. Needless to say, aiding and abetting for the purposes of Article 7(1) means aiding and abetting the perpetrators in the planning, preparation or executing -- execution of these crimes. But this means the planning, preparation, and execution of these crimes by the perpetrators. The Trial Chamber also feels confident in this decision by what is contained and what was dealt with in the pre-trial briefs and we refer the Prosecution to annex 1 of their own pre-trial brief, particularly to paragraphs 92 to 104, as well as to the pre-trial brief of the Defence at element 1.3. We also wish to refer you to the P562, so-called agreed facts document that was filed recently. I now come to instigating and I will deal first with the legal part of it. The Trial Chamber understands instigating as it has always been described by the various judgements of this Tribunal. With regard to the participants' conduct as element of the actus reus, instigating is prompting another to commit the offence. On the one hand, this needs more than merely facilitating the commission of the principal offence, as it may suffice for adding aiding and abetting, it rather requires some kind of influence the principal perpetrator by way of inciting, soliciting or otherwise inducing him or her to commit the crime. On the other hand, although the exercise of influence would hardly function without some sort of capability of impressing other -- other people, instigation, different from ordering, which implies at least a fact actual superior-subordinate relationship, does not presuppose any kind of superiority. Instigation can be performed by any means, both by express or implied conduct as well as by acts or omissions. Provided that in the latter case, under the given circumstances, the instigator is obliged to prevent the crime from being brought about. Instigation to war crimes needs either -- neither to be direct and public nor to require the instigator's presence at the scene of the crime. Thus instigating influence can be generated both face to face and by intermediaries as well as exerted to a smaller or larger audience provided that the instigator has the corresponding intent. The necessary link between the instigator instigating conduct and the principal crime committed commonly described as the causal nexus or causal relationship is not to be understood as requiring proof that -- requiring proof in the extent of a condicio sine qua non, it suffices that the instigation of the accused was a substantially contributing factor in the commission of the crime. Let me come to the facts and findings relating to instigating. Admittedly, the evidence adduced by the Prosecution to prove instigation by the accused for the commission of the crime of wanton destruction is not much. But for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the exercise required from this Trial Chamber is obviously less demanding and less heavy than the one it will have to do at the end of the trial when it will deliver judgement. For the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that there is evidence which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion that with regard to the attacks to which counts 5 refers, his alleged presence and participation, as well as his failure to try to prevent wanton destruction, when this was within his possibility, could amount to instigation. The Trial Chamber relies mainly on Exhibit P329, that is his own interview, on the testimony of Nedret Mujkanovic, that of Hakija Meholjic and also but particularly on the interview of the Accused. All in all, therefore, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that the Rule 98 bis standard has been reached for the purposes of the alleged allegation. The complete picture will of course be reviewed when we come to final judgement. Aiding and abetting. I'll start first with the legal outline of what we consider necessary. The Trial Chamber holds that aiding and abetting may be constituted by any contribution to the planning, preparation or execution of a finally completed crime provided that, on one hand, this falls short of one's own co-perpetration in the planning, instigation or ordering of the crime. And on the other hand, is substantially and efficient enough to make the performance of the crime possible or at least easier. Within this reach, any kind of physical or psychological, verbal or instrumental assistance or support regardless whether this is rendered directly to the perpetrators or by way of an intermediary as well as irrespective of whether the participant was present or removed both in time and place from the actual commission of the crime, may suffice as furthering or facilitating the performance of the crime provided that it was rendered before, during or after the principal act yet still prior to the full completion of the crime. To the same degree of ins -- as instigating, aiding and abetting can be fulfilled by express or implied conduct, as well as constituted by acts or omissions, provided that the latter -- in the latter case, under given circumstances, the Accused was indeed obliged to prevent the crime from being brought about. This can in particular become a -- very relevant in situations in which a person is aware of a crime to be committed while being present. However, participating in a crime does not require presence at the time and place when and where it is performed. While being present at the scene of a crime, without preventing it from occurring, does not per se constitute aiding and abetting. This holds only, however, as long as there is no duty to act as one may be derived -- as one may drive -- as it may be derived from a bystander's position of authority as a superior or actual leader. A similar situation is being expected to intervene -- a similar situation of being expected to intervene may arise when a person by his activities, has knowingly created the risk of enticing people to engage in criminal acts. If in such situations of higher authority and/or antecedent dangerous conduct, the presence on the scene of the offence is apparently even conceived of as an encouragement or approval of a crime about to be committed, it will be a short step beyond the border line from mere omission by failure to act to active aiding and abetting, if not even amounting to instigation. This can in particular apply to cases of an approving spectator or when the presence of a superior can be an important indicium for encouragement and support. With regard to the link between aiding and abetting and the principal crime committed in accordance with the case law of this Tribunal, the Prosecution is not required to prove that the principal crime would not have been committed were it not for aiding and abetting, still, however, as indicated by requiring a substantial or significant affect, the aiding and abetting contribution according to its supporting character must further or at least facilitate the commission of the crime. And we come to the findings. Once more, the same evidence that for the purpose of Rule 98 bis supports the charge of instigation within Article 7(1), individual criminal responsibility, sustains the charge of aiding and abetting the commission of the crime of wanton destruction under count 5. For the purpose of Rule 98 bis the Trial Chamber does not believe it needs to say more than this for the time being, and therefore comes to the conclusion that evidence has been adduced which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion beyond reasonable doubt that there has been aiding and abetting of -- on the part of the Accused of the crime of wanton destruction as charged in count 5. Conclusion, on counts 3 and 5. The Trial Chamber therefore comes to the conclusion that there is sufficient evidence upon which, if believed, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the Accused under Articles 3(B) and 7(3) and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal, that is of wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, not justified by military necessity. This being a violation of the laws and customs of war and which is brought against the accused in counts 3 and 5 of the indictment, with the exception of the villages of Radijevici and Bozici, for which no evidence has been adduced capable of sustaining a conviction. And we come to counts 4 and 6, namely plunder of public or private property. I just want to confirm, we haven't got much left. Can we proceed? I mean, do you have enough tape to proceed for another 15 minutes? I can't see. Okay. As we did in the case of counts 3 and 5, we will deal with these counts 4 and 6 together. The Prosecution has charged the Accused with the offence of plunder of public or private property, this being a violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Article 3(E) of the Statute of the Tribunal. In count 4 it is alleged that the Accused is criminally responsible as a commander pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for all incidents of plunder contained in the indictment. In counts 6, the Prosecution has charged the accused with individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute for the plunder that occurred during the attacks on Fakovici, and Kravica and Jezestica in which the accused is alleged to have participated in person. In paragraph 35 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that in the course of the attacks that I mentioned earlier, and which took place between the 10th of June 1992 and the 8th of January 1993, units under the command and control of Naser Oric plundered Bosnian Serb property, namely cattle, furniture, and television sets. According to the Prosecution, these incidents of plunder include all the villages and hamlets that I mentioned earlier. Two Appeals Chamber decisions deal with the crime of plunder. In Kordic, the Appeals Chamber concurred with the definition of that crime given by the Trial Chamber. Of course, the Trial Chamber in that case namely that the essence of the offence consists in all forms of unlawful appropriation of property in armed conflict for which individual criminal responsibility attaches under international criminal law including those acts traditionally described as "pillage." In Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber did not change the definition of plunder of property that had been reached by the Trial Chamber, namely that being the unlawful extensive and wanton appropriation of property belonging to a particular population whether it be the property of private individuals or of state or quasi-state public collectives. The position of the Trial Chamber is that for individual criminal responsibility to attach to plunder of public or private property as a violation of the laws or customs of war, pursuant to Article 3 of our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Statute, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the acquisition or appropriation of the property was, first, unlawful; second serious enough to reach the requirement of Article 1 of the Statute as a precondition to the Tribunal asserting jurisdiction; and third, intentional. The position of the Trial Chamber also is that the prohibition of plunder extends both to organised seizure of property under taken within the framework of a systematic economic exploitation and to acts of looting committed by undisciplined soldiers and individuals for private gain. The position of the Trial Chamber also is that as a violation of the laws or customs of war, plunder does not require the appropriation to be extensive or to have a large value. However, the question of value of property intentionally and unlawfully appropriated becomes relevant with regard to the jurisdictional requirement of Article 1 of the Statute of this Tribunal: The Trial Chamber therefore holds that to constitute a serious violation of international humanitarian law the appropriation must be of sufficient value as to involve grave consequences for the victims. It should, however, be noted that, in addition, plunder may constitute a serious violation, not only when one victim suffers severe consequence as a result of the unlawful appropriation, but also, for instance, when property of little value is unlawfully appropriated from a large number of people. It is the firm belief of this Tribunal, of this Trial Chamber that the seriousness of the violation must be ascertained on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration the specific circumstances of each case. As regards the mens rea of the crime of plunder, the Trial Chamber sees the mens rea as the intent to plunder, to appropriate intentionally and unlawfully of such property, which consists both of the knowledge and the will of the prescribed result and of the foreseeability of the consequences of the conduct and acceptance of the results as its very likely consequence. The question of necessity has been raised by the Defence in relation to this crime. This Trial Chamber holds that this Defence plea of necessity for the purpose of this case is only of merit when applied to the taking away of necessities which are needed in the context of preventing imminent starvation. The Trial Chamber also finds that the existence of a defence of necessity was an established principle of international -- in customary international law at the time the crime of plunder in counts 4 and 6 are alleged to have been committed. The Trial Chamber also takes the position that for the defence of necessity to succeed, in this case in relation to the crime of plunder, it needs to be satisfied that there was a present or imminent threat of severe and irreparable harm to life existence. Secondly the acts of plunder must have been the only means to avoid the aforesaid harm. Thirdly, the acts of plunder were not disproportionate. And lastly, the situation was not voluntarily brought about by the perpetrator himself. One last point I should like to make before I pass on to deal with the facts and findings part, is that although in the course of the oral submissions, the Prosecution suggested that the word furniture in paragraph 35 of the indictment does not and should not mean just furniture, but includes and should include all sorts of household goods and appliances, the Trial Chamber cannot agree with this. Furniture is furniture. That is those things which exist in a house or office that equip it in the usual connotation of furniture for living. The indictment itself doesn't consider a television set as being furniture. Consequently we fail to see any validity in the argument now put forward by the Prosecution that while a television set for the purpose of the indictment is not furniture, a radio or a tape recorder or a video recorder or a refrigerator or a pot or a pan should be considered as furniture. In this case, counts 4 and 6 of the indictment limit the alleged plunder to just three kinds of property, namely cattle, furniture, and television sets. Consequently, all the evidence relating to the appropriation of anything, such as weapons and ammunition, food clothing and household appliances, and medicines, will be ignored. Having premised all this, I shall now deal with the findings. And I repeat that our findings are unanimous. The Trial Chamber finds that there is abundant evidence which, if believed, could lead to the conclusion beyond reasonable doubt that during several of the attacks mentioned earlier, various heads of cattle were taken away, sometimes by fighters, most of the time by apparent civilians. As regards the alleged plunder of furniture and television sets, the only evidence that the Trial Chamber has been able to find is the following: First, during or following the attack on Ratkovici on the 27th of June 1992, Muslim soldiers were seen taking away all the household appliances from one house, which included a bed and a television set. The second instance that we have managed to come across is an alleged statement by the Accused himself on the 22nd of September 1992, during a meeting of the Srebrenica Operations Staff in which he stated that one of the biggest problems was how to protect property and that commanders like a certain Senahid, we've taken it to mean presumably Senahid Tabakovic had set a bad example to soldiers and civilians alike when he took away sofas during the attack on Bjelovac. The Trial Chamber makes it clear that in -- there is ample evidence which, if believed, could lead beyond reasonable doubt to the conclusion that there was massive plundering during these attacks, but as stated, its jurisdiction in this case is limited to the alleged plunder of cattle, furniture, and television sets, because it's only these objects that are mentioned in para 35 of the indictment on which counts 4 and 6 are based. After considerable thought on the law governing the crime of plunder, the defence of necessity and the jurisdiction of this Tribunal as spelled out in Article 5 -- Article 1 of the Statute, and of course the evidence that has been adduced, we come to the following conclusions. As regards the alleged plunder of cattle, although as I have stated already, there is ample evidence which, if believed, could lead beyond reasonable doubt that the conclusion that a few hundred heads of cattle were appropriated during or following the attacks, any individual criminal responsibility that could be attributed to the Accused under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute is offset by the real and present necessity that there was at the time to acquire immediately food for the survival of the population in Srebrenica which was under siege, completely surrounded and isolated and starving. The plunder of food, of which too there is abundant prima facie evidence in this case, has properly been omitted by the Prosecution for the counts -- purposes of counts 4 and 6, and the submission has been made that appropriating cattle is different from appropriating food, because cattle cannot be consumed in situ. Indeed, in theory, they are not the same, but the entire relevant evidence in there case indicates that what motivated the mass of people that were looting food and cattle was not what would usually characterise the crime of plunder but the urgent need for survival at a point in time when survival was critical, was vital, and this was the only possibility it seems that they had of acquiring food, amongst other things that were needed survival, such as clothing and medicines. The Trial Chamber has thought a lot. Obviously cattle cannot be quickly processed. The fact that cattle cannot be consumed on the site. Still cattle can be quickly processed into food, where it can be processed, and this could have and would have prevented or offset the starvation that the population was risking at the time. Prosecution seemed to have been more concerned with the fact that it could not be so processed on site, where it was. The Trial Chamber cannot agree with you. The Trial Chamber has thought a lot about coming to this conclusion and feels convinced that the Prosecution has failed to adduce evidence which could sustain a conviction for plunder of cattle and that all the requirements for the success of the plea of necessity as it relates to the alleged plunder of cattle are met, even though we want to make it clear that we have at no time considered that the onus of proof had shifted over the Defence. The onus of proof of plunder remained always on the Prosecution even for the purposes of Rule 98 bis. Under normal circumstances, the taking away of livestock or cattle would undoubtedly amount to plunder but in the extraordinary circumstances of this case, this appropriation of plunder together with food had become indispensable for the survival of the population of Srebrenica. The evidence brought forward by the Prosecution itself shows that not only was Srebrenica under siege, but that in the course of this protracted siege, the town was completely encircled and isolated and that the population which kept increasing in geometric proportions because of the influx of refugees was starving.
