In addition, there is always abundant evidence that in spite of the repeated calls for help and for supplies by the Srebrenica authorities, these never arrived precisely because the town was surrounded and isolated and, therefore, could never arrive in Srebrenica. It is finally pertinent to point out that there is no evidence to show that the plunder of cattle was disproportionate given the circumstances and, in addition, the evidence is such that there is nothing to show that the situation I have described in Srebrenica was voluntarily brought about by the persons concerned or by the perpetrators themselves. As regards the alleged plunder of furniture and television sets, the Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion that the evidence is so puny that although there is evidence that a bed, a sofa, and a television set may have been taken away, this does not rise to the level of seriousness which I mentioned earlier and which is related to the jurisdictional requirement of Article 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber might have decided differently had counts 4 and 6 not been limited to furniture and television sets, apart from cattle. Because of these conclusions and the decision that follows, there is no need for the Trial Chamber to go into other matters, legal or factual, related to counts 4 and 6. Our conclusion on counts 4 and 6. The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that for the purpose of these two counts the Prosecution has failed to adduce evidence capable of supporting a conviction for the crime of plunder of public or private property, a violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Article 3(E) of the Statute of this Tribunal and dulcis in fundo I now recapitulate all our conclusions in our decision. For the foregoing reasons, for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber unanimously comes to the following conclusions and therefore decides. 1: We enter a judgement of acquittal of the accused Naser Oric of the charges brought against him in counts 4 and 6 of the indictment, namely of the charge of plunder of public or private property, a violation of the laws and customs of war punishable under Articles 3(E), Article 7(3) and Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Our second decision orders the continuation of the case against the accused under the -- on the other counts, namely counts 1, 2, 3 and 5. However, it is being decided that the Accused need not address the alleged murder of Bogdan Zivanovic as regards count 1. And the alleged cruel treatment of Miloje Obradovic as regards count 2, for which there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction and for which he therefore cannot be held responsible. Furthermore, the accused need not address the alleged wanton destruction of the villages of Radijevici and Bozici, both in Bratunac municipality. As regards count 3 and count 5, for which there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction, and for which therefore, he cannot be held responsible. For practical purposes, although this is not an order, the Trial Chamber invites the Prosecution to present an amended version of the indictment to reflect these decisions. However, in so doing, please retain the number of -- the numbering of the counts. In other words, what was count 1 will remain count 1, what was count 2, count 3, count 4 will remain count 5 -- remain count 4, and count 5 will remain count 5, and count 6 will remain count 6. And as regards counts 3, counts 4 and 6 obviously you omit to mention anything else. This is our decision. I now suppose that the operators, technicians, need a short break. There is only one very minor thing that I need to address, and that is scheduling. I can do this in about three minutes. Shall I proceed or shall we break for five minutes? Seven minutes are plenty. Now, as you know, we have a task entrusted by the Rules. We need to schedule the beginning of the Defence case. I -- we have already had informally a discussion in my Chamber on this between the parties. More or less what I'm going to say is in agreement with what has been discussed with the parties and taking into account the exigencies of both -- particularly Defence counsel, the Defence counsel. Our first decision is the following: That no later than Friday, the 17th of June, the Defence is required to file the name or pseudonyms of each witness it intends to call. As well as a summary of the facts on which each witness called before the summer recess, that is, the recess starts on the 23rd of July. In other words, we require a summary of the facts on which each witness you will call before the 23rd of July and will testify. And then the points in the indictment as to which each witness called before the summer recess will testify. And the total number of witnesses and number of witnesses called -- to be called before the summer recess who will testify on each count. Similarly, as well, by the 17th of June, we need -- we require from you an indication of whether the witness or witnesses will testify in person or pursuant to Rule 92 bis, whether there will be a use of a transcript of testimony from other proceedings in this Tribunal. We also require an indication of the estimated length of time required for each witness and the total time estimated for the presentation of the Defence case. This is very important because we need to plan ahead. Finally, you need to file by the 17th June deadline a list of exhibits you intends to offer in this case, stating, where possible, whether the Prosecution has any objection as to their authenticity. The Defence is also supposed to or expected to serve copies on the Prosecutor of these exhibits but only with regard to the exhibits it intends to use during the testimonies of witnesses you intend to call before the summer recess. Then there will be a short break which will be utilised by you to finish this exercise, and we are giving you up to the 28th of June 2005 to file a summary of the facts which each remaining witness will testify about. The points of the indictment as to which each remaining witness will testify, the number of remaining witnesses that will testify on each count, and now as you know there are two less, and as you also are required then by 28th of June 2005 to serve on the Prosecution copies of the exhibits listed on 17th June, with the copies you intend to use during the testimonies of the remaining witnesses. Then we have already scheduled for you a meeting, a 65 ter meeting, on the 30th of June. This will be presided over by our Senior Legal Officer and this will be in terms of and pursuant to 65 ter, and this will be followed the day after, on the 1st of June, by -- 1st of July, by a full-blown Pre-Defence Conference in open session in this or in any other courtroom. This will be called -- convened pursuant to Rule 73 ter. Then you are expected to bring forward or, let me put it in other terms, to start your case on July 4th, which is a Monday. All right? I conclude by making a short statement. This has been the first experiment with the Rule 98 bis as it has been amended by the Judges in Plenary on the 18th of December of 2004. I think I can safely say that it has been a successful experiment. We have managed to start and conclude the whole exercise in less than a week, when, under previous -- under the previous regime it would have taken roughly between a month and a half and two months to conclude. It has spared you the burden of filing long and detailed written submissions. It has spared us having to prepare long, detailed judgements with annotations and all that. We have saved the Tribunal a lot of time and a lot of resources, which, as you can imagine, if multiplied by the existing number of cases and those which we hope will come in the future, means we have saved the Tribunal years and we have also served -- saved the Tribunal a lot of resources and money. I wish to thank you both because you have been a major contribution in enabling us to prove that the newly amended Rule 98 bis could work successfully. Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I wonder if I might just make a point very briefly. In fact, thank you, firstly, to the Chamber for your judgement, even if we respectfully disagree from some of the findings. We do naturally have to consider the possibility of requesting certification for appeal, but what I did want to say is that in light of the schedule outlined by Your Honour, if it turns out that we decide not to pursue that course, we of course reserve our right to take any of the points arising from the 98 bis judgements at the end of the trial. I wouldn't want it to thought that we would concede making any concessions that we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, taken for granted. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal agrees precisely with what -- and it has never been thought to be other wise. In other words, not appealing does not mean acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, in some cases it does and in this case not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not in our case. It's not. Yes. We stand adjourned. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.05 a.m.
